extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners and patent applicants/patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating obviousness rejections and the prior art (analogous art, content/timing of prior art, applicant replies, and consideration of rebuttal evidence) during patent examination. Covers tests, required findings, examples across technical arts, and procedural burdens for applicants and examiners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationales that may support a conclusion of obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of rationales that may support a conclusion of obviousness include: (A) Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results; (B) Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results; (C) Use of known technique to improve similar devices (methods, or products) in the same way; (D) Applying a known technique to a known device (method, or product) ready for improvement to yield predictable results; (E) 'Obvious to try' – choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, with a reasonable expectation of success; (F) Known work in one field of endeavor may prompt variations of it for use in either the same field or a different one based on design incentives or other market forces if the variations are predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art; (G) Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify the prior art reference or to combine prior art reference teachings to arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See KSR and MPEP § 2143 for discussion and examples illustrating how the cited rationales may be used to support a finding of obviousness; see MPEP §§ 2144–2144.09 for additional guidance regarding support for obviousness determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's reply requirements under 37 CFR 1.111(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once Office personnel have issued a rejection that establishes the Graham factual findings and concludes that the claimed invention would have been obvious, the burden shifts to the applicant to (A) show that the Office erred in these findings or (B) provide other evidence to show that the claimed subject matter would have been nonobvious. 37 CFR 1.111(b) requires applicant to distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable over any applied references. An effective traverse of a rejection based wholly or partially on Office factual findings must include a reasoned statement explaining why the applicant believes the Office has erred substantively as to the factual findings. A mere statement that the Office has not established a prima facie case or that reliance on common knowledge is unsupported by documentary evidence is not substantively adequate under 37 CFR 1.111(b). Office personnel may repeat the rejection and make the next Office action final if traverse is inadequate (see MPEP § 706.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of affidavits/declarations and statutory exceptions to overcome prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant's reply could establish that a disclosure relied on in an obviousness rejection is not prior art in view of a 35 U.S.C. 102(b) exception, or that subject matter, although prior art, is disqualified for use in an obviousness rejection in view of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §§ 2146, 2153.01, 2154.02 and § 2155 regarding affidavits or declarations under 37 CFR 1.130 (and for pre-AIA cases 37 CFR 1.131/1.132) to overcome prior art rejections; see MPEP §§ 716–716.10 regarding traversing grounds of rejection with affidavits/declarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant's rebuttal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all rebuttal evidence that is timely presented by applicants when reevaluating any obviousness determination. Rebuttal evidence may include evidence of 'secondary considerations,' such as 'commercial success, long felt but unsolved needs, [and] failure of others,' and may also include evidence of unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After rebuttal evidence is presented, Office personnel should reconsider the initial obviousness determination in view of the entire record (see In re Piasecki; In re Eli Lilly & Co.). The Office action should clearly communicate the Office’s findings and conclusions, articulating how the conclusions are supported by the findings. All rejections of record and proposed rejections should be reviewed for continued viability. Follow procedures in MPEP § 706.07(a) when determining whether an action may be made final. See MPEP § 2145 for consideration of rebuttal evidence and MPEP §§ 716–716.10 for affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 for use in 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter that is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 can be used to support a rejection under section 103. Admitted prior art can be relied upon for both anticipation and obviousness determinations, regardless of whether the admitted prior art would otherwise qualify under statutory categories of 35 U.S.C. 102.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it is established that a disclosure does not qualify as prior art under the appropriate section of 35 U.S.C. 102, then that disclosure is not prior art that can be used in an obviousness rejection. For instance, a 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) reference overcome by a declaration under 37 CFR 1.130(a) cannot be used in an obviousness rejection for a claimed invention subject to 35 U.S.C. 102; similarly for pre-AIA cases and 37 CFR 1.131. See MPEP §§ 901–901.06(d), §§ 2121–2129, and §§ 2151–2155 for overviews of what constitutes prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive content of the prior art (enabling disclosure, inoperative devices, admissions, scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing prior art, consider issues such as availability of inoperative devices, extent to which prior art must be enabling, whether a prior art disclosure is broad disclosure rather than preferred embodiments, and admissions by the applicant or others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §§ 2121–2129 for case law and guidance relating to these substantive content issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine prior art content at the relevant time to avoid hindsight
rubrics_metrics.description: Content of the prior art is to be determined as of the relevant time (before the effective filing date for AIA applications; at the time of the invention for pre-AIA) to avoid impermissible hindsight. Decisionmakers should 'cast the mind back' to what a person of ordinary skill knew at that time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2145 (subsection X.A.) for discussion of rebutting applicants' arguments that a rejection is based on hindsight. Citations include W.L. Gore v. Garlock and other precedent recognizing the need to view prior art from the vantage of one skilled in the art at the relevant time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) common ownership/joint research agreement requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 who wants to rely on pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) to overcome an obviousness rejection has the burden of establishing that prior-art subject matter used in the rejection and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person. For joint research provisions, the applicant must establish: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the invention was made; (B) the invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These disqualifications apply only for subject matter which only qualifies as prior art under subsections (e), (f), or (g) of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and is used in a rejection under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a). Note limitations for certain filing/grant dates (e.g., applications filed prior to Nov. 29, 1999). See MPEP § 2146.02 for requirements to establish common ownership or a joint research agreement and MPEP § 2146.01 for related limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art requirement for use under 35 U.S.C. 103
rubrics_metrics.description: To rely on a reference under 35 U.S.C. 103, the reference must be analogous art to the claimed invention. A reference is analogous art if: (1) it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if it addresses a different problem); or (2) it is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if not in the same field). It is not necessary for a reference to fulfill both tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must determine whether a reference is analogous art when analyzing obviousness. There is no analogous-art requirement for a reference being applied in an anticipation rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102. See In re Bigio and related case law; when more than one prior art reference is used, the references need not be analogous to each other (see Sanofi-Aventis; Corephotonics). Consider the disclosure of each reference 'in view of the reality of the circumstances' and from the vantage of common sense likely to be exerted by one of ordinary skill in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying the 'reasonably pertinent' test — consider the inventor's problem and factual basis
rubrics_metrics.description: For the 'reasonably pertinent' test, the examiner should consider the problem faced by the inventor as reflected in the specification (explicitly or implicitly). A reference outside the field of endeavor is reasonably pertinent if a person of ordinary skill would have consulted it and applied its teachings when faced with the inventor's problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To support a determination that a reference is reasonably pertinent, the examiner may include a statement of the examiner's understanding of the problem and factual reasons why the prior art is pertinent to the identified problem. The question often turns on how the problem is perceived; a narrow/constrained view inconsistent with the specification may inappropriately limit the scope of available prior art. See In re ICON Health and Fitness; In re Clay; In re Klein; Airbus; Donner Tech. and related authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider similarities and differences in structure and function
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating whether a reference is analogous art or pertinent, similarities and differences in structure and function of the inventions disclosed in the references carry far greater weight than Patent Office classifications or cross-references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should focus on structural similarities and functional overlap between references and the claimed invention when weighing analogy. See In re Ellis and examples provided where structural/functional overlap made references pertinent despite classification differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art examples across technical arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples illustrating analogous art in various technical fields: chemical arts (references concerned with absorbing biologically active materials on carriers were pertinent to preservative particulate compositions), mechanical arts (broad prior art inquiry into other areas where similar problems exist; toothbrushes analogous to hair brushes where function/structure overlap), electrical arts (solutions to rate-limiting problems in high-power devices applicable to pacemaker design), and design arts (see MPEP § 1504.03 for design analogous-art case law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples show application of the analogous-art tests in different arts and underscore that prior art from different fields may be pertinent if problems/functions align; see cited cases (Ex parte Bland; Stratoflex; In re Mlot-Fijalkowski; Stevenson; In re Bigio; Medtronic v. Cardiac Pacemakers; etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences between prior art and the claimed invention — consider the claim as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims requires interpreting the claim language and considering both the invention and the prior art references as a whole. The question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is not whether the differences themselves would have been obvious, but whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §§ 2111–2116.01 for case law pertaining to claim interpretation and MPEP § 2143.03 for examples of claim language that may raise questions as to limiting effect. Case law (e.g., Stratoflex, Schenck) supports treating the claimed invention holistically in obviousness analysis.
